title: Pests, contamination and hygiene triage
audience: Coordinators, support workers and trained cleaners who may be asked to work in a home affected by hoarding or environmental neglect, as part of an authorised support plan. Not a qualification or authority to clear a property, dispose of a resident's belongings, enter by force, or provide welfare or clinical support.
learningOutcomes: Record pest and contamination indicators as observations, not diagnoses.
Restrict access and avoid aerosol-producing actions in a described scene.
Route the case to the specialist named in the plan.

instruction.heading: Scope of this lesson
instruction.body: This lesson covers recognition, access restriction and referral. It does not cover pest treatment, decontamination, or the disposal of contaminated goods, and completing it does not qualify a worker to undertake them.

instruction.heading: What to observe
instruction.body: Droppings, insects, mouldy goods and unknown liquids can signal contamination that ordinary cleaning does not manage. The WA Department of Health mould guidance advises against dry brushing, because dry brushing breaks the fungi up into small fragments. This module applies the same caution to mouldy goods found in a hoarded home: do not disturb the material to see more. Note the location, the extent and the odour from outside the affected area. Record what you see. Do not name a pest or a contaminant, because identification belongs to the specialist.

instruction.heading: Restrict access and refer
instruction.body: Restrict access to the affected area and keep residents and other workers out until guidance is in place. Avoid dry sweeping, vacuuming and any action that creates dust or aerosols. Do not open sealed containers or probe enclosed spaces. Record the indicators as observations, keep the record dated, and route the case to the specialist the plan names. Pest and contamination decisions belong to specialists.

procedure: Stop at the doorway. Note the location, the extent and what can be seen from outside.
Do not disturb droppings, mouldy goods or unknown liquids, and do not probe enclosed spaces.
Avoid dry sweeping, vacuuming and any action that creates dust or aerosols.
Restrict access to the area and keep residents and workers out until guidance is in place.
Route the case to the specialist named in the plan, with the indicators recorded.
Record each observation as an observation, not a diagnosis, and keep the record.

workedExamples.situation: A sealed storage room has a strong odour and visible droppings.
workedExamples.reasoning: Restrict access, avoid any aerosol-producing action and do not open the room further. Record the indicators as observations and request a specialist risk evaluation.

workedExamples.situation: A worker is asked to vacuum the droppings so the room can be used.
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Vacuuming can spread particles. Decline, record the request and refer it to the coordinator and the specialist.

equipmentAndPpe: Hazard log with fields for location, extent and observed indicators.
Barrier tape and signage for the restricted area.
Training-only photographs and mock records. No real droppings or contaminated goods are handled in this lesson.

commonErrors.error: Dry sweeping or vacuuming droppings or mouldy goods.
commonErrors.prevention: Restrict access and avoid aerosol-producing actions until approved guidance is obtained.

commonErrors.error: Describing an observation as a diagnosis, such as naming a pest.
commonErrors.prevention: Record what was seen, and let the specialist identify it.

commonErrors.error: Opening sealed containers to see what is inside.
commonErrors.prevention: Leave them closed, record them and refer.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Pest control, contamination and decontamination are restricted to competent and, where required, licensed people. Completing this lesson does not qualify a worker for them.
The WA mould guidance is written for buildings in Western Australia. Its advice against dry brushing is applied here as a precaution, not as a hoarding standard.

qualityStandard: The learner records indicators as observations, without naming a pest or a contaminant.
The learner restricts access and avoids aerosol-producing actions in a described scene.
The learner routes the case to the named specialist.
documentationEvidence: Hazard log with location, extent and observed indicators, dated.
Access-restriction record and referral to the named specialist.
summary: Observe from outside, and do not disturb.
No dry sweeping or vacuuming of droppings or mouldy goods.
Refer pests and contamination to the specialist.

knowledgeChecks.question: Droppings and mouldy goods are found in a sealed storage room. What is the correct approach?
options: Dry sweep the droppings and bag the goods.
Restrict access, avoid aerosol-producing actions and obtain approved guidance.
Open the windows and clean as usual.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which record is correct for a suspected pest problem?
options: 'Pest identified as rodents; treat with bait.'
'Room is pest-free after a quick sweep.'
'Droppings observed near the wardrobe; specialist assessment requested.'

knowledgeChecks.question: A resident asks the crew to vacuum the droppings to make the room usable. What is correct?
options: Decline, record the request and refer it to the coordinator and the specialist.
Vacuum them quickly, because the resident asked.
Vacuum them with the door open for ventilation.

WA Department of Health, Guidelines for managing mould and dampness: related public health risks in buildings, April 2024 edition, section 4.2.2, read 2026-11-03. Dry brushing is advised against there. Applying that to hoarded goods is a module precaution, not a statement in the guideline.

officialReferences.title: Guidelines for managing mould and dampness: related public health risks in buildings (WA Department of Health)
officialReferences.pageDate: April 2024 (version control table); publication code ENV-0014702 MAY'24; no separate last-updated date shown
officialReferences.covers: Read through a page-summary tool on 2026-11-03 (PDF, Environmental Health Directorate, WA Department of Health). Section 1.4 sets out a general public health duty, a workplace duty and a residential tenancies duty. Section 2.1 names people with existing respiratory, immunocompromising and allergic conditions, and infants, children and older people. Section 3.2.2 says porous items are often not economically salvageable and must be thrown out. Section 3.3 says the source must be located to address the cause and prevent recurrence. Section 3.4.1 defines simple contamination as new, isolated and visible, no greater than one square metre, with easily identified causes, and its footnote calls the one-square-metre size arbitrary. Section 3.4.2 defines complex contamination as larger than one square metre or found in multiple rooms or places. Section 3.5 states there are no defined quantitative or qualitative exposure thresholds for mould or dampness. Section 4.1 lists containment, drying and source repair as principles. Section 4.2.2 advises scrubbing hard surfaces with soapy water, avoiding dry brushing, cleaning at least 30 to 50 cm beyond the visible mould, removing or discarding porous items that cannot be adequately cleaned, stating that mould is not considered hazardous waste, and not painting, sealing or covering surfaces until dry. Section 4.3 recommends a site-specific plan with professionals for complex contamination, isolation with heavy grade plastic and negative pressure, and evacuation of occupants. Section 4.4 lists no recurrence within two to four weeks after remediation as an indicator of success, recommends the evaluation be done by a different entity, and states there are no legal requirements for a post-remediation assessment. Appendix B recommends a P2 or N95 respirator and says PAPRs should be used for complex remediation. Appendix E says mould can grow within 24 to 48 hours in flood-affected homes.

moduleAuthority.heading: Module authority and restricted work
moduleAuthority.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to enter a home by force, to clear, sort or dispose of a resident's belongings without valid consent, to handle or dispose of hazardous waste, to deal with unstable stacks or structural hazards, or to provide welfare, clinical or safeguarding assessments. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate or approval. Work is done only under an authorised support plan and a written agreement with the resident, within the limits set by the employer and the local law. Tenancy, safeguarding and information-sharing rights are jurisdiction-specific, and fire-risk, structural, pest and hazardous-waste decisions belong to the competent authorities and specialists named in the plan. Where authority or consent is unclear, stop and refer.

stopWorkAndReferral.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
stopWorkAndReferral.body: Stop and refer whenever any of these is true: consent is not specific, documented and current; the resident has objected or withdrawn consent; a party seeks entry by force, nonconsensual disposal or removal of personal documents; a fire-load, ignition, egress or obstruction hazard is present; a stack or structure is unstable; pests, unknown liquids or mouldy goods are present; sharps, chemicals or unknown containers are found; waste would go to general disposal without characterisation; private information is requested without authority; or the work would go beyond the approved plan. Stopping is a valid professional outcome. Record the disagreement, protect the resident's choices and refer the authority dispute before any property is moved.
